Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (CNN) -- The United Arab Emirates has refused to grant a visa to a female Israeli tennis player, preventing her from competing in the Sony Ericsson World Tennis Association Tour in Dubai, the WTA said in a statement Sunday. The UAE has refused to grant a visa allowing Shahar Peer to compete in Dubai. Shahar Peer would have been the first Israeli athlete to participate in a professional sporting event in the UAE, CNN Sports correspondent Pedro Pinto said. The UAE has no diplomatic ties with Israel. Peer told CNN on Sunday evening she was "very, very disappointed" to be denied access to the tournament. "Any player that qualifies should attend, and I was prevented," she said from Israel. "I'm glad the WTA support me. A red line was crossed for every athlete in the world -- politics should be kept separate from sports." The governing body of women's tennis said it was "deeply disappointed" that Peer was being denied entry to the country hosting the tournament, but it did not cancel the competition, which began Sunday. The move runs counter to WTA policy, which says no player should be barred from competing in a tournament for which she has qualified. Dubai could lose its membership in the WTA tour next year over the ban on Peer, according to WTA rules. That would mean professional players could compete only in exhibition matches in Dubai, the results of which would not count in pro rankings. Government officials in Dubai have not responded to CNN's request to comment over their refusal to allow Peer to compete in the event. "Ms. Peer has earned the right to play in the tournament, and it is regrettable that the UAE is denying her this right," said Larry Scott, chairman and chief executive of the tour.  Watch Scott express disappointment » . "Following various consultations, the tour has decided to allow the tournament to continue to be played this week, pending further review by the tour's board of directors." The patron of the Dubai Tennis Championships is Dubai's ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Makhtoum. Two million dollars in prize money is on the line. Al-Makhtoum told CNN in 2004 that Dubai would accept Israeli students to a school dedicated to students from the Middle East who are talented at sports. In 2003, Dubai hosted World Bank and International Monetary Fund meetings, which Israeli government officials attended. The Israeli flag -- among other member states' flags -- is still part of a globe monument in Dubai. Peer, 21, is ranked 48th in the world among female tennis players. She was allowed to compete at the Doha tournament in Qatar last year, where she received a warm welcome, according to Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz. Qatar, another Gulf Arab state, froze diplomatic ties with Israel after Israel's military offensive in Gaza last month. Peer downplayed the political undertones of her participation in last year's Doha tournament, telling Haaretz that she didn't come to Qatar "to help the politics of course." But she added that if her playing in the tournament "can help for peace or anything, I'd be really happy." Scott said the tour will "review appropriate remedies for Ms. Peer" as well as "appropriate future actions with regard to the future of the Dubai tournament." Peer was advised Saturday by tournament and WTA officials of the denial of her visa while she was participating in a tournament in Pattaya, Thailand, according to a WTA statement. The Dubai Tennis Championships runs through February 28.

Under those regulations, Dubai could be removed from the WTA Tour the following year. If that happened, professional players in Dubai would be limited to exhibition contests whose results would not affect official rankings.

Dubai government representatives did not respond to CNN’s request for comment on the decision.

Larry Scott, the tour’s chairman and chief executive, said Peer had earned her place in the competition and described the UAE’s refusal to admit her as regrettable.

“Following various consultations, the tour has decided to allow the tournament to continue to be played this week, pending further review by the tour’s board of directors,” Scott said.

Dubai ruler Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Makhtoum serves as patron of the Dubai Tennis Championships, which offers $2 million in prize money.

Israel’s flag, together with those of other member countries, also remains displayed on a globe monument in Dubai.

Peer, 21, was ranked 48th among the world’s female tennis players. The previous year, she had been permitted to compete in Doha, Qatar, where she received a warm reception, according to the Israeli newspaper *Haaretz*.

Qatar, another Arab Gulf nation, suspended diplomatic ties with Israel following Israel’s military operation in Gaza the month before.

At the time of the Doha event, Peer sought to minimize the political significance of her appearance. She told *Haaretz* that she had not traveled to Qatar “to help the politics of course,” but added that she would be “really happy” if her participation could contribute to peace or anything similar.

Scott said the WTA would consider “appropriate remedies for Ms. Peer” and determine “appropriate future actions with regard to the future of the Dubai tournament.”

According to the WTA statement, tournament and tour officials informed Peer on Saturday that her visa had been rejected while she was competing in Pattaya, Thailand.

The Dubai Tennis Championships was scheduled to continue through February 28.

# UAE Visa Ban on Shahar Peer Puts Dubai Tennis Tournament’s Future at Risk

**DUBAI, February 2009** — The United Arab Emirates’ refusal to admit Israeli tennis player Shahar Peer has triggered a confrontation with the Women’s Tennis Association, raising the possibility that Dubai’s prestigious tournament could be fined, sanctioned or removed from the professional calendar.

Peer, then one of Israel’s leading players, had qualified to compete in the Dubai Tennis Championships but was denied a visa shortly before the event began. The decision left her unable to enter the country and forced her withdrawal from the tournament.

## Why the UAE refused entry

At the time, the UAE did not have diplomatic relations with Israel and generally did not admit travelers using Israeli passports. Relations were especially tense after Israel’s military offensive in Gaza, which ended only weeks before the tournament.

Dubai tournament officials said authorities were concerned that Peer’s presence could provoke demonstrations or create a security risk. Organizers argued that television images of the Israeli player competing in Dubai might inflame public anger over the Gaza conflict.

Tournament director Salah Tahlak said officials feared that Peer’s participation could lead to protests and potentially expose players and spectators to danger. The visa decision was made by UAE immigration authorities rather than by the WTA, although the tournament remained responsible under Tour rules for ensuring that qualified players could enter the host country.

The WTA rejected the idea that nationality or political tensions justified excluding a player. Peer had earned her place through her ranking and had entered the event through the same process as other competitors.

## WTA condemns “discriminatory” treatment

WTA chief executive Larry Scott strongly criticized the visa refusal, saying the Tour would not tolerate discrimination against a player based on nationality.

The WTA had previously sought assurances that all eligible players would be permitted to compete in Dubai. Because the denial came shortly before play began, however, the organization chose not to cancel the event immediately. Many players had already arrived, and the tournament draw and preparations were complete.

Scott said allowing the competition to proceed did not amount to approval of the UAE’s action. The WTA launched a formal review and warned that Dubai had placed its future on the women’s calendar in jeopardy.

Peer also criticized the decision, saying sport should not be used as an instrument of politics. Several leading players expressed sympathy, though most continued to compete.

American star Venus Williams, who went on to win the tournament, said she believed Peer deserved to play and emphasized that professional tennis should remain open to athletes from every country.

## Commercial and political fallout

The dispute quickly spread beyond the WTA.

The Tennis Channel in the United States canceled its planned coverage of the women’s tournament in protest. *The Wall Street Journal Europe* withdrew its sponsorship, saying it could not support an event that excluded a player because of her nationality.

The controversy also affected the men’s tournament held in Dubai the following week. American Andy Roddick, the defending champion, withdrew and said he did not agree with the decision to deny Peer entry.

Faced with mounting international criticism and the risk of further damage, UAE authorities granted a visa to Israeli men’s player Andy Ram, allowing him to compete in the men’s doubles event. That decision reduced the prospect of a second confrontation but did not resolve the dispute over Peer.

## Consequences Dubai could face

Under WTA rules, tournaments are expected to provide equal access to all eligible players. Failure to do so can be treated as a breach of the tournament’s agreement with the Tour.

Possible penalties included:

- A substantial financial fine  
- Loss of ranking or sanctioning status  
- Removal from the WTA calendar  
- Requirements to provide advance visa guarantees  
- Compensation for Peer  
- A guaranteed place for her in a future tournament  
- Damage to sponsorship and international broadcast agreements  

The most serious threat was the loss of the event itself. Dubai had invested heavily in becoming a major stop on the international tennis circuit, offering significant prize money and attracting many of the world’s top players. Removal from the calendar would have damaged both the tournament and the emirate’s effort to present itself as a global sports and business center.

## WTA ultimately imposes a record penalty

The WTA later imposed a record **$300,000 fine** on the Dubai tournament. Part of the penalty was designated as compensation for Peer, including an amount tied to the prize money she might reasonably have earned.

Dubai was also required to provide written assurances well in advance that any Israeli player who qualified for future editions would receive a visa. The Tour further required that Peer be offered entry into the next tournament even if her ranking would not otherwise have secured her a place.

The WTA stopped short of removing Dubai from the calendar, reflecting the event’s importance, the large field already assembled and the UAE’s subsequent decision to admit Andy Ram. But the punishment established that host governments could not use diplomatic disputes to determine which qualified players were permitted to compete.

The episode became one of professional tennis’s most prominent clashes between international sport and Middle Eastern politics. It also demonstrated that Dubai’s status as a major tournament host depended not only on prize money and facilities, but on guaranteeing access to players regardless of nationality.
